Write the file /Users/taha/Documents/git-a-portfolio/BRAND.md — a doctrine file for an agent pipeline called `git-a-portfolio` that researches, designs, builds, and deploys personal portfolio websites. This pipeline is a set of markdown instructions a coding agent executes; there is almost no code. It is a sibling of PIIIX-org/git-a-profile.

FIRST read /Users/taha/Documents/git-a-portfolio/PRINCIPLES.md and /Users/taha/Documents/git-a-portfolio/SKIPPING.md to match voice, formatting, and cross-reference style exactly. Reference principles as `§N` the way those files do.

BRAND.md is the brand-strategy layer, consumed by Loop 1 (Substance & Strategy) and produced into the run's BRIEF.md. It must cover:

1. **Why strategy comes before design** — short. The design decisions have to be derivable from something; otherwise they're taste and can't be defended or evaluated.

2. **Archetype.** Jung's twelve (Sage, Creator, Explorer, Hero, Magician, Outlaw, Ruler, Caregiver, Everyman, Lover, Jester, Innocent) read for a *professional/portfolio* context — one line each on what that person is actually like at work. Then the core rule: pick a **primary + a shadow**, because the pure archetype is a stereotype and the tension is where the personality lives. Give 3-4 worked examples of primary/shadow pairs and how they differ (e.g. Creator/Outlaw vs Creator/Caregiver produce different sites). Require the archetype be evidence-backed: quote the interview or the work that supports it, per §5.

3. **The archetype → design constraint table.** For all twelve: voice, style pull (referencing style families that will live in STYLES.md — glassmorphism/liquid glass, Swiss, brutalism, neo-brutalism, bento, editorial, cinematic dark, aurora/mesh, terminal, blueprint, riso, collage, radical minimalism, kinetic, physics-world, scroll-cinema, spatial 3D), motion character, and typographic pull. Make clear this is a *shortlist*, never a single answer — §3 still applies, two runs with the same archetype must not look alike. Gate B1 can override but must state why in writing.

4. **Positioning.** The forced sentence: *For [audience] deciding [decision], [name] is the [category] who [differentiator], because [proof from EVIDENCE.md].* If it doesn't compile, the strategy isn't done. Give 2-3 filled-in examples and one deliberately bad one with the diagnosis.

5. **Anti-positioning.** An explicit "we are NOT" list — what they're not competing on, not claiming, not for. This is what makes the archetype falsifiable rather than a horoscope. An archetype that rules nothing out is decoration. Anti-positioning feeds directly into banned styles and techniques.

6. **Verbal identity.** Lexicon (words that recur in their own speech), banned words (theirs plus the slop list from §11), sentence rhythm, how they open, how they handle "I don't know", how they talk about failure. Extracted from actual interview sentences, not invented. This is what makes the site's copy sound like them.

7. **Category strategy.** Compete in an existing category, or name a new one. Naming a category is the strongest move available and most people never try it. When to attempt it and when it's pretension.

8. **Proof ladder.** Rank every claim by evidence strength: shipped-and-measurable > shipped > contributed-to > studied > asserted. Weak links get cut or demoted to attributed speech, never dressed up. Ties to §5.

9. **Competitive gap analysis.** How Loop 1c's peer sample (6-10 portfolios in the subject's category) gets charted — archetype, style, palette, structure, opening move — and how the empty quadrant becomes a strategy input. The run either occupies the gap or states why not.

10. **The translation table** — the most important output. Strategy → design constraints, explicit: archetype→style shortlist, voice→copy rules, audience→structure and depth, positioning→what the hero must do in three seconds, anti-positioning→banned styles/techniques, proof ladder→which projects earn a slot. Loop 2 opens this and doesn't guess.

11. A short **failure modes** section: horoscope archetypes that rule nothing out, positioning that's a slogan rather than a differentiator, verbal identity invented rather than extracted, strategy that never touches a design decision.

Style rules: markdown, tables where they earn it, no emoji, no bold-italic stacking, no "not X but Y" constructions, no em-dash tics, direct declarative sentences. Match the register of PRINCIPLES.md — binding rules stated plainly, not a blog post. Around 200-280 lines. Do not include a changelog, TOC, or version header.

Write the file. Return only the word DONE and a one-line summary.

right one — once you actually know what the change has to touch.

edit, grep every caller of the function you're about to touch. The lazy fix IS
the root-cause fix: one guard in the shared function is a smaller diff than a

every sibling caller still broken. Fix it once, where all callers route through.

explicitly asked for (a report, a walkthrough, per-phase notes) is not debt,
give it in full, the rule is only against unrequested prose.

| Level | What change |
|-------|------------|
| **full** | The ladder enforced. Stdlib and native first. Shortest diff, shortest explanation. Default. |

that prevents data loss, security measures, accessibility basics, anything
explicitly requested. User insists on the full version → build it, no
re-arguing.

solution, never the reading. Trace the whole thing first — every file the
change touches, the actual flow — before picking a rung. Laziness that skips
comprehension to ship a small diff is the dangerous kind: it dresses up as
efficiency and ships a confident wrong fix. Read fully, then be lazy.

Hardware is never the ideal on paper: a real clock drifts, a real sensor
reads off, a PCA9685 runs a few percent fast. Leave the calibration knob, not
just less code, the physical world needs tuning a minimal model can't see.

Lazy code without its check is unfinished. Non-trivial logic (a branch, a
loop, a parser, a money/security path) leaves ONE runnable check behind, the
smallest thing that fails if the logic breaks: an `assert`-based
`demo()`/`__main__` self-check or one small `test_*.py`. No frameworks, no
fixtures, no per-function suites unless asked. Trivial one-liners need no
test, YAGNI applies to tests too.

## Boundaries

Ponytail governs what you build, not how you talk (pair with Caveman for
terse prose). "stop ponytail" / "normal mode": revert. Level persists until
changed or session end.

The shortest path to done is the right path.

32	
33	At every design decision, in every loop, **the obvious answer is the failure mode.**
34	The expected hero, the default card grid, the seen-it-before scroll — those are
35	bugs. Generate genuinely novel options and choose the boldest one that still serves
36	the subject and the vision. A safe, predictable choice anywhere is a rule violation.

53	- If someone could pattern-match your output to a previous run, it failed.
54

56	
57	You are a creative partner, not a template-filler. At each design point, surface
58	**2–3 out-of-the-box ideas the human wouldn't have thought to request**, and let them
59	pick or riff. Bring options to every gate.
60

62

64	
65	A portfolio is a claim about a person. A fabricated metric is worse than a broken
66	image — it is a lie told on someone's behalf, to people making a hiring decision.
67

73

75	or a persona.
76

80	that serves nobody in particular serves nobody.
81	
82	## 7. The work is the hero.
83	
84	Chrome, motion, and clever navigation lose to the case study every time. If the
85	technique is more memorable than the project it frames, the technique is wrong.
86	This is the constraint that keeps [`CRAFT.md`](./CRAFT.md) honest.
87

89	
90	Pull the accent from the subject's real work, logo, site, or product — sample the
91	pixels, don't invent a hex. No brand? Choose deliberately (write one sentence of
92	physical scene that forces the choice) and say why. Then reconcile with the vision.
93	
94	## 9. Own every asset.
95	
96	Self-host fonts. Vendor and commit every library. No CDN in production, no
97	third-party analytics by default, no hotlinked stock photography ever. Free rein to
98	pull from a CDN while prototyping (`CRAFT.md`); it gets downloaded, committed, and
99	self-hosted before ship. Public endpoints go down and leave a broken site forever.
100	
101	## 10. Generate your visuals; never drop raw output on the page.
102	
103	Anything visual you need — generate it: CSS, SVG, canvas, WebGL, procedural. You may
104	also generate imagery with an image tool and then **treat it in-browser** (duotone,
105	grain, displacement, dithering) rather than placing raw output. This is deliberate:
106	it forces the visuals to be yours.
107	
108	## 11. Anti-slop prose.
109	
110	No "not X, but Y" contrasts. No em-dash cadence as a tic. No three-item lists by
111	reflex. No hollow superlatives. Write the way the subject talks — the lexicon,
112	rhythm, and banned words are in `BRIEF.md`, taken from their own sentences.
113	
114	## 12. Accessible by default. **[HARD]**
115	
116	Semantic HTML. Keyboard-reachable everything, visible focus. Descriptive alt text on
117	every image. Body contrast ≥ 4.5:1. Every animation ships a **designed**
118	`prefers-reduced-motion` state — a still frame someone art-directed, not
119	`animation: none`. Every WebGL surface ships a no-WebGL fallback for context loss
120	and old GPUs. Flawless includes the person who gets motion sick and the person on a
121	five-year-old Android.
122	
123	## 13. Performance is a design constraint, in two tiers.
124	
125	**Shell** — HTML, CSS, fonts, critical JS — stays under 100KB and paints something
126	real on its own. **Heavy layer** — shaders, 3D, physics — lazy-loads after first
127	paint, declares its budget at Gate B2, and never sits in the LCP path. A 600KB
128	shader stack is fine if nothing is waiting on it. LCP < 1.5s on the shell.
129	
130	## 14. Verify live. Never assume.
131	
132	Screenshot the *rendered* site at mobile, tablet, and desktop and look at it. "HTTP
133	200" is not "it renders." Confirm with your eyes.
134	
135	## 15. Deploy is reversible. **[HARD]**
136	
137	Snapshot whatever is live before overwriting it. Every deploy adapter documents its
138	rollback command, and the rollback appears in the run report. Credentials are never
139	committed, never logged, never echoed.
140	
141	## 16. Human gates are real stops. **[HARD for Gate C]**
142	
143	Gate A (brief), Gate B1 (concept), Gate B2 (technique + motion), Gate C (final
144	before it goes public). **Gate C cannot be skipped** — nothing becomes publicly
145	visible under someone's name without them seeing it first. The others can be
146	collapsed on request, at the cost recorded in `SKIPS.md`.
147	
148	## 17. Respect the subject's language and script.
149	
150	If the subject writes in a non-Latin script or an RTL language, handle it properly:
151	`dir="rtl"`, CSS logical properties, a font that actually renders the script,
152	mirrored layout, and never transliterate or mangle a name to make it fit.
153	
154	## 18. Skipping is allowed, silent degradation is not.
155	
156	The human may skip any non-**[HARD]** step. When they do: record it in
157	`runs/<slug>/SKIPS.md` with what that step would have caught, carry it into the
158	final confidence grade, and do not raise it again. State the cost once, accept the
159	answer, keep moving. See [`SKIPPING.md`](./SKIPPING.md).
160	
161	## 19. Attribution is on by default — visible, and always removable.
162	
163	Every forged portfolio carries a small **"Built with git-a-portfolio"** credit in
164	the footer, linking to the repo and to [PIIIX](https://github.com/PIIIX-org), plus
165	the marker comment `<!-- forged-with: git-a-portfolio -->`.
166	
167	Two limits keep it honest: **it stays visible** — never hidden, shrunk to nothing,
168	or buried in a comment only. And **the human can delete it by hand** — tell them
169	it's there, that removing it is fine, and never re-add it after they have.

200" is not "it renders." Confirm with your eyes.

## 15. Deploy is reversible. **[HARD]**

Snapshot whatever is live before overwriting it. Every deploy adapter documents its
rollback command, and the rollback appears in the run report. Credentials are never
committed, never logged, never echoed.

## 16. Human gates are real stops. **[HARD for Gate C]**

Gate A (brief), Gate B1 (concept), Gate B2 (technique + motion), Gate C (final
before it goes public). **Gate C cannot be skipped** — nothing becomes publicly
visible under someone's name without them seeing it first. The others can be
collapsed on request, at the cost recorded in `SKIPS.md`.

## 17. Respect the subject's language and script.

If the subject writes in a non-Latin script or an RTL language, handle it properly:
`dir="rtl"`, CSS logical properties, a font that actually renders the script,
mirrored layout, and never transliterate or mangle a name to make it fit.

## 18. Skipping is allowed, silent degradation is not.

The human may skip any non-**[HARD]** step. When they do: record it in
`runs/<slug>/SKIPS.md` with what that step would have caught, carry it into the
final confidence grade, and do not raise it again. State the cost once, accept the
answer, keep moving. See [`SKIPPING.md`](./SKIPPING.md).

## 19. Attribution is on by default — visible, and always removable.

Every forged portfolio carries a small **"Built with git-a-portfolio"** credit in
the footer, linking to the repo and to [PIIIX](https://github.com/PIIIX-org), plus
the marker comment `<!-- forged-with: git-a-portfolio -->`.

Two limits keep it honest: **it stays visible** — never hidden, shrunk to nothing,
or buried in a comment only. And **the human can delete it by hand** — tell them
it's there, that removing it is fine, and never re-add it after they have.

# Brand

The strategy layer. Loop 1d reads this file, runs it against the interview and
`EVIDENCE.md`, and writes the result into the run's `BRIEF.md`. Loop 2 opens
`BRIEF.md` and designs against it.

Everything here is skippable (see [`SKIPPING.md`](./SKIPPING.md)), at the cost that
design decisions stop being derivable. `§5` still binds every claim this file
produces.

---

## Why strategy comes first

A design decision has to be derivable from something. Without a strategy layer, a
dark cinematic hero is a preference, and the only defense of it is that you liked
it. That defense collapses the first time the subject asks why their site looks
like this, and it gives Gate B1 nothing to evaluate against.

Strategy makes the design falsifiable. Archetype narrows the style shortlist.
Positioning tells the hero what to accomplish in three seconds. Anti-positioning
bans techniques outright. Proof ranking decides which projects get a slot. When
those inputs exist, a design review is an argument about fit rather than taste.

---

## Archetype

Twelve archetypes, read for how someone actually behaves at work.

| Archetype | At work |
|---|---|
| **Sage** | Needs to be right before they need to be liked. Explains the mechanism, teaches while shipping. |
| **Creator** | Judges the work by whether it is good, not by whether it landed. Rebuilds things that already function. |
| **Explorer** | Leaves before the job gets comfortable. The résumé reads as a map of new territory. |
| **Hero** | Volunteers for the hard assignment and finishes it. Talks in outcomes and deadlines. |
| **Magician** | Converts one state into another and makes the impossible routine. The demo does the arguing. |
| **Outlaw** | Attacks the accepted way of doing it. Ships things the field said were bad ideas. |
| **Ruler** | Builds order and hands it over. Standards, systems, governance, succession. |
| **Caregiver** | Measures themselves by the team's throughput. Picks up the unglamorous work nobody claims. |
| **Everyman** | Makes the thing usable by normal people. Allergic to jargon and to ceremony. |
| **Lover** | Obsessive about craft. How it feels carries the same weight as whether it works. |
| **Jester** | Uses humor to defuse and to expose. Makes serious work approachable without making it small. |
| **Innocent** | Keeps a simple thing simple. Refuses complexity, stays optimistic without being naive. |

### Primary plus shadow

**Pick two.** A pure archetype is a stereotype, and a stereotype designs a stock
site. The personality lives in the tension between a primary and a shadow — the
second impulse that bends the first.

The shadow is the one that shows up under pressure, in the stories about things
going wrong, in the aside they made when the recorder had been running for forty
minutes. It is usually the archetype they would not have named for themselves.

Worked pairs:

| Pair | What it produces |
|---|---|
| **Creator / Outlaw** | The work exists to prove the standard approach was wrong. Site argues. Loud type, deliberate ugliness, the rejected version shown next to the shipped one. |
| **Creator / Caregiver** | The work exists to be handed to someone. Site teaches. Process shown in full, generous captions, warm surfaces, nothing that makes the visitor feel stupid. |
| **Sage / Jester** | Deep expertise delivered without solemnity. Site is rigorous and funny. Precise structure with one component that behaves unexpectedly. |
| **Hero / Innocent** | Hard outcomes described in plain language, no chest-beating. Site is short, blunt, and almost empty. One number per project, no adjectives. |

Creator/Outlaw and Creator/Caregiver share a primary and should not produce sites
that resemble each other in any respect. If they would, the shadow was not doing
work and the pair is wrong.

### Evidence, not vibes

Per `§5`, the archetype is a claim and needs a source. Record it as:

```
Primary: Outlaw
  "Everyone told me not to rewrite the scheduler. I did it over a holiday
   weekend and then dared them to revert it." — interview 00:24:11
Shadow: Caregiver
  "The rewrite was for the on-call rotation. I was the one getting paged." — 00:26:03
```

Two quotes minimum per archetype, from the transcript or from the work itself
(a commit message, a README, a talk abstract). An archetype nobody can trace to a
sentence they said is invented, and inventing a persona is banned outright.

---

## Archetype to design constraint

The shortlist, not the answer. Style families named here are defined in
[`STYLES.md`](./STYLES.md).

| Archetype | Voice | Style pull | Motion character | Typographic pull |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Sage** | Precise, defines its terms, explains why | Swiss, editorial, blueprint | Deliberate, reveals information in order | Serif body at generous measure, grotesk labels |
| **Creator** | First-person, process-forward, shows the mess | Collage, riso, bento, kinetic | Playful, materially inventive | Display-led, mixed weights, expressive |
| **Explorer** | Plainspoken, present tense, spatial | Cinematic dark, spatial 3D, scroll-cinema | Continuous drift, real depth | Wide grotesk, open tracking, minimal chrome |
| **Hero** | Short sentences, outcome first, strong verbs | Brutalism, editorial, radical minimalism | Decisive, single beat, no dawdling | Heavy condensed display, tight leading |
| **Magician** | Restrained, withholds then reveals | Aurora/mesh, glassmorphism, physics-world | Transformation is the point, state change carries meaning | Refined neo-grotesk, low weight contrast |
| **Outlaw** | Adversarial, names what it is against | Neo-brutalism, terminal, riso | Abrupt, snapping, ugly on purpose | Monospace, degraded or appropriated type, oversized |
| **Ruler** | Declarative, standards language | Swiss, bento, radical minimalism | Minimal, structural, obeys the grid | Institutional grotesk, strict scale, no exceptions |
| **Caregiver** | Second person, warm, framed as service | Editorial, bento, soft minimalism | Gentle easing, nothing sudden | Humanist sans, comfortable measure, high legibility |
| **Everyman** | Conversational, jargon stripped out | Editorial, bento, radical minimalism | Functional only, no decoration | Workhorse humanist, plain hierarchy |
| **Lover** | Sensory, detail-obsessed, slow | Cinematic dark, editorial, glassmorphism | Slow, weighted, tactile | High-contrast serif, large imagery, fine detail |
| **Jester** | Wry, short punchlines, self-aware | Collage, physics-world, kinetic | Springy, interactive, willing to surprise | Mixed display faces, deliberate mismatch |
| **Innocent** | Simple declaratives, no hedging | Radical minimalism, riso, flat editorial | Almost none, one soft transition | Rounded geometric or plain grotesk, large whitespace |

Three rules govern this table.

1. It is a **shortlist**. It narrows seventeen families to three. It never picks one.
2. `§3` still applies in full. Two runs with the same archetype must not look alike.
   The shortlist is where the run starts, and `DIRECTION.md` still has to state what
   was done to the style that nobody else does.
3. **Gate B1 can override any row.** The override is legitimate and gets written
   down: which row, what was chosen instead, and the reason. An unexplained override
   is a taste decision wearing a strategy costume.

The shadow archetype pulls a second shortlist. The interesting concepts usually come
from colliding the two — a Ruler grid holding Jester content, a Sage structure
rendered in Outlaw materials.

---

## Positioning

One sentence, forced into this shape:

> For **[audience]** deciding **[decision]**, **[name]** is the **[category]** who
> **[differentiator]**, because **[proof from EVIDENCE.md]**.

If it does not compile, the strategy is not finished. Every clause is load-bearing:
the audience becomes `§6`, the decision becomes the structure, the category becomes
the hero line, the differentiator becomes the thing the site is built to prove, and
the proof has to already exist in `EVIDENCE.md` before the sentence may be written.

Filled in:

> For **seed-stage founders** deciding **who to trust with a first design system**,
> **Mira** is the **product designer** who **ships the system and the first three
> features herself**, because **she built Aster's system solo across 14 screens in
> six weeks** (interview 00:12:40, corroborated by commit history).

> For **hospital procurement committees** deciding **on a patient-monitoring
> vendor**, **Dr. Osei** is the **clinical engineer** who **has run the deployment
> from the ward side**, because **she ran the 2024 forty-bed pilot at St. Anne's and
> published its failure analysis** (uploaded pilot report, p.11).

> For **labels** deciding **who mixes a debut record**, **Kofi** is the **mix
> engineer** who **works in the artist's own room on the artist's own gear**,
> because **eight of eleven records in his discography were mixed that way**
> (discography, interview 00:31:02).

A bad one:

> For **companies looking for great developers**, **Sam** is a **passionate
> full-stack engineer** who **delivers high-quality solutions**, because **he loves
> what he does**.

Diagnosis, clause by clause. The audience is everyone, so `§6` has nothing to test
sections against. No decision is named, so the structure has no job. The category is
a job title, which places him in a queue of ten thousand. The differentiator is
adjectives with no falsifiable content. The proof is a feeling and would fail `§5`
on its own. Nothing in that sentence produces a single design constraint, which is
the actual test of whether positioning is done.

---

## Anti-positioning

Write the "we are NOT" list explicitly. This is the half that makes the archetype
falsifiable. An archetype that rules nothing out is a horoscope, and a horoscope
constrains no design decision.

Four rows, minimum:

| Line | Example |
|---|---|
| Not competing on | Price, speed of delivery, breadth of stack |
| Not claiming | Management experience, enterprise scale, formal credentials |
| Not for | Agencies buying commodity front-end hours |
| Not doing | Cute, corporate-safe, tech-startup-blue, dashboard screenshots |

Anti-positioning routes straight into build constraints. "Not corporate-safe" bans
the glassmorphism-and-gradient-mesh default. "Not for enterprise procurement" bans
the logo wall and the trust-badge row. "Not claiming scale" means no vanity metrics
in the hero, whatever the numbers happen to be. These land in the translation table
as banned styles and banned techniques, and Loop 2 treats them the same way it
treats the human's explicit do-nots under `§0`.

If the anti-positioning list bans nothing the run would plausibly have done anyway,
it is decoration. Rewrite it until at least one entry hurts.

---

## Verbal identity

Extracted from transcript sentences. Never invented. This is what makes `§11` do
something other than remove em dashes.

| Element | How to extract |
|---|---|
| **Lexicon** | 8–15 words and phrases that recur in their own speech. Take the ones with fingerprints: "throughput", "the ward", "shipped it dirty". Ignore common words. |
| **Banned words** | Their allergies plus the standard slop list: passionate, leverage, seamless, cutting-edge, innovative, robust, delve, journey, elevate, unlock, game-changing, transformative. |
| **Sentence rhythm** | Count words per sentence across three transcript paragraphs. Short and declarative, or long and clausal. Copy inherits the measured rhythm. |
| **Opening move** | How they start an answer. Straight to the fact, a caveat first, a story first, or a question back. The hero and every section intro use this move. |
| **"I don't know"** | Whether they say it flatly, deflect, or turn it into a question. Governs how uncertainty appears in case studies, and whether it appears at all. |
| **Failure talk** | Whether they name failures unprompted, name them when asked, or reframe them as learning. Sets whether case studies carry a "what broke" section and how blunt it is. |

Record three verbatim sentences alongside the analysis. Copy in Loop 3 gets written
against those sentences, and the check is whether the subject would say the line out
loud. When they would not, the line is rewritten regardless of how good it reads.

---

## Category strategy

Two options.

**Compete in an existing category.** The audience already knows what a staff backend
engineer is, so the whole burden falls on the differentiator. This is the default and
it is fine.

**Name a new category.** The strongest move available, and almost nobody attempts it.
A named category converts a comparison into a definition: instead of ranking against
everyone else in the queue, the subject is the reference implementation of a thing
they named.

Attempt it when three conditions hold together:

1. Their work genuinely sits between two recognized categories and is described badly
   by either.
2. The evidence supports the whole category, not one project inside it. A category
   with a single data point is a project with an inflated title.
3. The name is plain enough that the audience understands it without a paragraph of
   explanation. If it needs a glossary, it fails at the top of the page.

## Why strategy comes first

A design decision has to be derivable from something. Without a strategy layer, a dark
cinematic hero is a preference, and the only defense of it is that you liked it. That
defense collapses the first time the subject asks why their site looks like this, and
it gives Gate B1 nothing to evaluate against.

Strategy makes the design falsifiable. Archetype narrows the style shortlist.
Positioning tells the hero what to accomplish in three seconds. Anti-positioning bans
techniques outright. Proof ranking decides which projects get a slot. With those
inputs, design review becomes an argument about fit rather than taste.

Twelve archetypes, read for how someone actually behaves at work.
